root.name: Dutch Defense: Alekhine Variation
root.moves: 1. d4 f5 2. c4 Nf6 3. g3 e6 4. Bg2 Be7 5. Nf3 O-O 6. O-O Ne4

overview: In the fianchetto Classical Dutch Black plays 6...Ne4, placing a knight on the strong e4 outpost. White replies with 7.Nbd2 or 7.d5, challenging the knight and fighting for the centre. Black prepares ...d6, ...Qe8 and ...Bf6 or ...Nc6, with kingside chances based on the f5 pawn.

white_ideas.idea: Challenge e4 with Nbd2 and Qc2
Gain space with d5 or e3 and Qc2
Pressure the c-file and exchange the e4 knight

black_ideas.idea: Keep the e4 knight and play ...d6, ...Qe8

typical_structures.structure: Classical Dutch with e6, f5 and d6 against d4 and c4

character.notes: Both sides have clear plans but the f5 move leaves weaknesses and the game is double-edged.

gambit.notes: No material is given up in the main line.

soundness.notes: A mainline Dutch set-up and sound.

structure.notes: The centre stays tense with chances to open either side.

approach.notes: A main line of the Dutch, played now and then by strong players.

level.notes: The Dutch needs a deep sense of when to push f4 or ...d5.

sublines_that_differ.name: Alekhine, 7.d5
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 f5 2. c4 Nf6 3. g3 e6 4. Bg2 Be7 5. Nf3 O-O 6. O-O Ne4 7. d5
sublines_that_differ.how: White gains space instead of challenging the knight.

character.reason: The Dutch is known for unbalanced, double-edged positions with attacking chances for both sides.

structure.reason: The centre has not locked and either side can open it.

level.reason: The plans matter more than lines, and the middlegame takes judgement.

plans.reason: The knight on e4 and the g2 bishop give both sides targets.
